references.text: The same principle that everything that touches the altar shall become holy is mentioned in connection with the burnt offering altar.
The law concerning the sin offering confirms that anything that touches the sacrificial meat shall be holy.
Repeats the principle that whatever touches the holy flesh becomes holy.
Describes the anointing of the altar so that it becomes most holy.
Warns the sons of Kohath against touching the holy objects, which underscores the holiness of the objects.
Ezekiel describes that the priests shall not go out into the outer court with their holy garments, lest they make the people holy.
Haggai raises a question about the transfer of holiness through contact.
Jesus speaks of the altar as making the gift holy and refers to the principle that the holy transfers holiness.
The principle that holy objects transfer sanctity to what they touch (or are eaten by), illustrated through the priests' right to eat the most holy offerings.
A concrete application of the principle in Exodus 30:29 by listing which offerings are considered 'most holy' and belong to the priest.
Theological connection through the expression 'I am the Lord who sanctifies them,' where Leviticus confirms God's role in the process described in Exodus.
Direct parallel: Both verses formulate the same theological principle that contact transfers holiness (from priests in Ex 30, from sacrificial meat in Lev 6).
